note.text: A network map represents nodes and links. Its legend identifies modes; link labels can give distances independently of the drawing’s scale. A route must use connected open links. When transfers are explicitly allowed, different modes can form a route. For a distance comparison add the distances of its links; do not infer time or fare without further data.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to read a network legend and select a shortest open route with working. Builds on: network links, transfers and constraints. Leads to: trade flows and volume.

sections.heading: Follow the local example or model
sections.text: The invented map uses solid roads and dashed rail links. Transfers at nodes are allowed. With no closure, A–B–D totals {10}+{15} = {25} km and A–C–D totals {20}+{15} = {35} km. The top route is shorter in this example. Other practice maps change distances or close a link. These are invented models, not travel instructions.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Record each link’s mode and distance. Cross out any route containing a closed link; total each remaining route. State the shortest open listed route and its distance. Explain why a shorter-looking drawing or a non-existent direct link is not evidence.
